analysis.one_liner: Replaces Clean Water Act wetland permits with a looser three-tier system and pays landowners for the most protected wetlands.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 181 House cosponsors from both parties and held two subcommittee hearings, but never reached a House vote before the 102nd Congress ended in January 1993.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have rewritten Section 404 of the Clean Water Act, the main federal permit program for filling or draining wetlands. It would have sorted wetlands into three classes: the most ecologically important (Type A) would mostly be off-limits, but the government would buy them from owners at fair market value; moderately important ones (Type B) could be developed with mitigation; and a large "Type C" category could be developed with no permit at all. It would also use a stricter test for what counts as a wetland, exempt many farming and mining activities, presume permits granted if the Army Secretary misses a six-month deadline, and cap the most-protected category at 20% of any county. It died in committee without a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Owners and would-be developers of wetland property — real estate developers, farmers, timber and ranching operations, and oil, gas and mining interests — gain most: many wetlands would leave federal jurisdiction entirely, permitting would be faster and friendlier to applicants, and owners of the most restricted wetlands could sell them to the government at full fair market value plus attorneys' fees.

how_it_helps.text: Wetlands serving only 'marginal' functions, prior converted cropland, and wetlands in developed areas would be classified Type C and could be drained, excavated or filled without any federal permit [S2][S3].

The bill sets a strict definition: land counts as a wetland only if surface water is present at least 21 consecutive days during the growing season, which would remove many seasonally wet lands from regulation [S3].
If the Army Secretary fails to act on a permit application within six months, the permit is presumed granted on the applicant's own terms [S3].

Owners of Type A wetlands could demand compensation at fair market value — calculated without counting any value lost because of the regulation and possibly including attorneys' fees — and title would pass to the United States [S2][S3].

Normal farming, ranching, silviculture and aquaculture activities, farm and forest roads, aggregate and clay mining with reclamation, and prior converted cropland would all be exempt from permitting [S2][S3].

analysis.who_pays: The public. Wetlands store floodwater, filter water, and support fisheries and wildlife; the stricter definition, the unregulated Type C category, and the presumed-permit rule would weaken those protections nationwide. Taxpayers would also fund the fair-market-value purchases of Type A wetlands from private owners, and courts could award attorneys' fees on top.

drawbacks.text: Environmental and Clean Water Act defenders argued the bill would gut federal wetland protection: the 21-day surface-water test, the broad Type C exemption, the county-level 20% cap on Type A designations, and the presumed-permit rule would all shrink the scope of regulation [S2][S3].
State or local land management plans approved by the Secretary could exempt activities from permitting, and no person would be entitled to judicial review of those approval decisions [S3].

The good-faith case for the bill: the existing Section 404 program was not designed as a wetland regulator and could leave private owners of 10+ acres holding land they could not use or sell, with no compensation; the bill offered a predictable process, deadlines, appeal rights, and full payment for the most restricted land [S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill would have given landowners real, paid-for relief from a permit program they called unpredictable and confiscatory. The cost, by the record of its own text, was a narrower federal safety net: thousands of seasonally wet acres would leave protection, permitting would default to approval when deadlines lapse, and the public's flood-control and water-quality benefits would erode while taxpayers financed buyouts. Weighing a nationwide public good against compensation for a concentrated set of landowners, the design tilts toward the landowners.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in two House committees, got two subcommittee hearings, and never received a committee vote or floor vote before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Jimmy Hayes of Louisiana introduced the bill on March 7, 1991, and it was jointly referred to the Merchant Marine and Fisheries and Public Works and Transportation committees [S1][S5].

It gathered 181 cosponsors — 115 Republicans and 66 Democrats — and federal agencies including the Army Corps of Engineers, EPA, Interior, Agriculture, and Commerce were asked for their views [S4][S5].
Subcommittees held hearings in November 1991 and May 1992, but neither full committee ever approved the bill, and the House never voted on it before the 102nd Congress ended January 3, 1993 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Because it died without a vote, the existing Clean Water Act wetland permit rules stayed in force; the public keeps current flood-control and water-quality protections, while landowners and developers gained nothing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Wetlands protections and the public relying on them

sides.party_line_note: Support crossed party lines: 115 of 167 House Republicans and 66 of 267 House Democrats cosponsored, and the sponsor was a Louisiana Democrat.

industries.note: The bill would shrink regulated wetlands through a stricter definition and a broad Type C exemption, speed up permitting, and presume approval when the government misses its deadline. Fewer permit fights mean cheaper, faster development on lands that now provide flood storage and water filtration for nearby communities.

Normal farming, ranching, silviculture and aquaculture activities, farm and forest roads, prior converted cropland, and even cranberry bog expansion would be exempt from permitting, freeing growers to convert seasonally wet acreage without federal review.

A taking of Type A wetlands would generally cover surface interests only, leaving subsurface oil, gas, and mineral rights accessible — and denial of access would itself count as a compensable taking. Aggregate and clay mining with reclamation would be exempt outright.

The bill would require a state mitigation banking program in every state, creating a market for firms that restore or create wetlands and sell credits to permit applicants. The public benefit depends on those banks actually replacing lost wetland functions, which regulators would have to enforce.
